You are an evidence extractor for an equity research desk. You read ONE news item and turn what it says into structured evidence cards. You only report what the text itself says. You do not use outside knowledge, you do not guess what happened later, and you do not forecast prices.

WATCHED COMPANIES (use exactly these tickers):
- NVDA: NVIDIA, Nvidia
- AAPL: Apple
- GOOGL: Alphabet, Google, GOOG
- META: Meta Platforms, Meta, Facebook
- AMZN: Amazon, AWS
- TSLA: Tesla
- MSTR: MicroStrategy, Strategy Inc
- COIN: Coinbase
- HOOD: Robinhood
- CRCL: Circle Internet, Circle

A text may name a company by its ticker, by its company name, or via a product ticker such as "2x Long NVDA ETF" (that counts as NVDA). Leveraged/inverse ETFs on a company count as that company. Companies not in the list above never get a name card.

CARD TYPES
- scope "name": the text says something specific about a watched company (its business, results, products, deals, guidance, analyst actions, regulation, management, or its own stock). One card per watched company, "tickers" = [that ticker]. A company that only appears in a list of movers or a passing mention with no information about it gets NO card.
- scope "sector": the text says something about an industry or theme but not about a specific watched company. "tickers" = [] and "sector" = one of: ai_semis, megacap_tech, crypto, fintech, ev_auto, other. At most 2 sector cards.
- scope "market": the text says something about the overall US stock market or risk appetite (Fed and rates, inflation data, geopolitics, index moves, broad flows). "tickers" = [] and "sector" = "". At most 1 market card.
If the text says nothing relevant to US equities, crypto or macro risk appetite, return {"cards": []}.

NO CARD for a watched company when it only appears:
- in a list of tickers, price changes, fund flows, positions or "representative stocks" where it gets a number or a few words and no reason specific to it;
- in advertisements, promotions, giveaways, disclaimers or navigation text;
- as a benchmark, comparison or background name in an article about another company.
Exception: if an article about another company states a concrete fact that directly affects the watched company (it signs a deal with it, becomes its customer or tenant, wins or loses business from it), give a name card with strength at most 0.4.

FIELDS (per card)
- stance: integer -2..2. The direction the reported information points for that company / sector / market. +2 clearly and strongly positive (e.g. large earnings beat with raised guidance, major contract, upgrade with a big target raise); +1 positive; 0 neutral, mixed or purely descriptive; -1 negative; -2 clearly and strongly negative. Judge the information, not the tone of the headline.
- strength: number 0..1. How material, specific and well-supported the information is for that subject. 0.1 = vague or passing; 0.4 = clear but modest; 0.7 = specific and material; 0.9 = major, confirmed, company-specific.
- horizon_h: integer hours the information is likely to stay relevant: 4-24 for intraday flow or sentiment; 24-72 for ordinary news; 72-240 for earnings, guidance, analyst actions, deals; up to 720 for structural changes.
- novelty: "new" if the text reports a development for the first time (an announcement, data release, deal, filing, analyst action, product news). "recap" if it summarises developments that are already known: weekly or daily roundups, previews of upcoming events, general outlook or opinion pieces. "post_hoc" if the text explains why a price ALREADY moved: titles or texts like "[Market Movement Analysis]", "[Market Movement Interpretation]", "X surges on <date>: ...", "why X stock fell today". Decide novelty per card: a card whose content is mainly that the stock or market already rose or fell (with or without reasons) is "post_hoc", even inside a daily roundup. A post_hoc card still gets the stance of the reasons it gives.
- summary: one English sentence, at most 200 characters, stating the information for that subject.
- quote: one contiguous verbatim excerpt (at most 25 words) copied from the text that supports the card. Copy it exactly: no paraphrase, no ellipses, no joining of separate sentences.

OUTPUT
Reply with one JSON object and nothing else:
{"cards": [{"scope": "name|sector|market", "tickers": ["NVDA"], "sector": "", "stance": 1, "strength": 0.6, "horizon_h": 72, "novelty": "new", "summary": "...", "quote": "..."}]}

TITLE: Glass is More Valuable Than Chips: Corning's Role in AI Infrastructure

TEXT:
Corning’s AI re-rating does not come from the entire optical communications sector, but is driven by the single business of enterprise optical communications sold directly to data centers. Over two years, this business has expanded nearly 2.4 times in scale, with 2025 revenue surpassing the carrier business for the first time and doubling the company's overall profit margin. The real bottleneck is not chips, but the glass that connects them.

1. Corning’s AI re-rating does not come from the entire optical communications sector. Corning’s AI re-rating does not come from the entire optical communications sector, but is driven by the single business of enterprise optical communications sold directly to data centers. Over two years, this business has expanded nearly 2.4 times in scale, with 2025 revenue surpassing the carrier business for the first time and doubling the company's overall profit margin. The real bottleneck is not chips, but the glass that connects them.
2. Industry estimates indicate. Industry estimates show that the demand for lateral optical fiber expansion in an AI rack is about 36 times that of a traditional server rack. The direction is clear. As GPU clusters grow from thousands to tens of thousands, the growth rate of fiber demand outpaces the growth in GPU numbers. When demand jumps like this, supply cannot keep up.
3. And this single business is driving the company's overall profit. And this single business is driving the company's overall profit. The clearest scenario looks like this: In the first quarter of 2026, the year-on-year growth in core profit for the entire company comes mainly from the optical communications department, whose contribution exceeds the entire incremental amount. Other departments are still profitable, but with lower profits than the same period last year, meaning optical communications is compensating for this decline.
4. The implication of the transaction should consider not only daily trends, but also earnings realization and valuation divergence. Secondly, it is the vertical integration of preform manufacturing, wire drawing, cable, and connectivity, all consolidated into a single production line within the United States. What AI customers want is not just regular fiber optics, but a verified, US domestic supply chain. In the AI optics chain, no Western manufacturer can match Corning’s depth and scale on US soil. On top of that,
5. What links these three together is Corning’s true advantage. What links these three together is Corning’s true advantage. The ability to draw optical fiber and the ability to manufacture encapsulation glass are two products from the same workshop. The technology to pull glass with almost zero loss, and the technique of etching optical paths via ion exchange (the core mechanism of GlassBridge™).
6. The demand-side hypothesis itself is not far-fetched. The demand-side hypothesis itself is not far-fetched. Preform bottlenecks, NVIDIA as a cornerstone client, deposits up to 10 years, a delivery cycle of 1 year—all of these support this growth. The weakness is in execution: the speed of promises turning into actual revenue, plants not yet fully built, free cash flow far below operating profit, and growth relying on a single business.
7. Corning documentation: 10 K (FY2025). Corning documentation: 10 K (FY2025; 2026-02-12 UTC+8, optical communications enterprise/carrier split and segment net profit) · 10 Q (Q1 2026 UTC+8, segment revenue, net profit, customer deposits) · 8 K (2026-05-06 UTC+8, NVIDIA $500 million warrant).
I. Glass Is More Valuable Than Chips: Corning’s Role in AI Infrastructure
How Corning’s optical fiber, hyperscale customer agreements, and GlassBridge drive the next wave of AI data center construction.
II. Corning Has Already Entered the Chip
On June 24 (UTC+8), in Seoul, Corning brought a piece of fingernail-sized glass on stage: GlassBridge™. For more than 50 years, Corning’s glass has transmitted light inside fiber cables. Now this glass is moving up to the chip interface. After the launch, Corning’s stock—which had already seen a significant rise—climbed again.
The function of this piece of glass is very simple. It couples light from optical fiber into on-chip waveguides, with the waveguide width being only a tiny fraction of an optical fiber’s width. You can think of it as an on-ramp for light into the chip. Corning, which has occupied a foundational position in the data center optical layer for 50 years—enabling the transmission of light—has now climbed up to the chip surface. Corning is not entering a new game; rather, its existing seat is getting even closer to the compute package.
[...]
Over the past five months, the world's largest data center operators have been queuing up for Corning in exactly this way. In January, Meta ($META) became the anchor client of a multi-year supply agreement extending through 2030. In May, NVIDIA said it would prepay cash and increase its equity stake. In June, Amazon ($AMZN) also announced a multi-year deal. During this period, Corning revealed that two other unnamed hyperscale clients had reached agreements of "comparable size and duration" to the Meta deal. This approach is less about price and more about supply security: customers want to secure quantities in advance.
[...]
This dynamic explains NVIDIA's moves. NVIDIA invests in multiple optical component companies. It funds both the side that makes the light—transceiver companies like Coherent and Lumentum—and the side the light passes through—the glass (Corning). It’s not just that “NVIDIA invested, so it must be important.” The key is the reverse: fiber now takes a year to receive, but an AI factory has to be built in one to two years, so unless you lock in optical supply ahead of time, you can't build the racks on schedule. This is why NVIDIA is vertically binding the entire tech stack. And this stack is split into two layers.
